title: Hojicha: What It Is, What It Tastes Like, and How It Differs From Matcha

seo.title: Hojicha: What It Is, Taste, and Hojicha vs. Matcha
seo.meta_description: Hojicha is roasted Japanese green tea with nutty, caramelized, woody aromas and less grassy character than matcha. It is usually brewed with very hot water and also works well with milk.
seo.search_intent: Understand what hojicha is, how it is produced, what it tastes like, how to brew it, and how it differs from matcha.

excerpt: Hojicha is Japanese green tea that is roasted after initial processing. Heat transforms its profile: it loses much of the vivid grassy character associated with matcha and develops roasted aromas reminiscent of nuts, caramel, and wood. It is commonly brewed with hotter water and is also popular in lattes and desserts.
content_html:
Hojicha is Japanese green tea that is roasted after its initial processing, and that roasting dramatically changes its color and aroma. Instead of the green, marine, vegetal profile associated with many Japanese teas, hojicha develops toasted notes that can resemble nuts, wood, light cocoa, grain, or caramel.

It can be made from leaves, stems, or a combination. One well-known style, Kaga bōcha, relies heavily on tea stems and uses specific roasting methods to develop fragrance.

Roasting is the central difference

Japanese green teas are heated early in processing to stop enzymatic oxidation. Hojicha receives an additional high-temperature roasting stage afterward. That heat creates new aromatic compounds and darkens the tea material to brown shades.

Although it begins as green tea, a finished cup does not look like bright sencha or vivid green matcha.

What does hojicha taste like?

Japan's agriculture ministry describes hojicha as fragrant and roasted with relatively little bitterness or astringency. Depending on raw material and roast level, you may notice cereal, nut, caramel, woody, or lightly smoky notes.

This flavor profile pairs particularly well with milk. Official Japanese recipes even use hojicha in chai-style drinks with hot water, milk, and cinnamon.

Hojicha and matcha are not two versions of the same powder

Matcha is produced from tea leaves cultivated and processed specifically for very fine grinding. The powder is suspended in water and the leaf material itself is consumed.

Hojicha is traditionally sold as roasted leaves or stems that are steeped and removed, although powdered hojicha now exists for lattes and baking. The fact that both can appear as powders today does not make their processing or flavor equivalent.

The color already hints at the flavor difference

Matcha retains chlorophyll and appears vividly green. Hojicha loses much of that green appearance during roasting and becomes brown. The visual change accompanies real heat-driven aromatic chemistry.

In a latte, matcha creates bright green color, while hojicha produces beige to light-brown tones and a flavor closer to toasted grain or mild coffee.

How is hojicha brewed?

Japan's Ministry of Agriculture recommends very hot water, around 90–100°C/194–212°F, for roasted teas and short steeps around 30 seconds to one minute. High temperature helps release the roasted aroma.

A traditional Kaga bōcha guide uses roughly two tablespoons tea for 300 ml boiling water and about 25 seconds. Variety and cut still affect intensity, so producer instructions remain useful.

Does hojicha have less caffeine than matcha?

Japanese sources describe hojicha as relatively low in caffeine, but no single number applies to every cup. Leaf or stem choice, tea amount, extraction time, and temperature all matter.

Matcha is consumed as whole powdered leaf, meaning the serving includes all of the tea material used. A precise caffeine comparison therefore requires actual quantities rather than beverage names alone.

Why is hojicha growing now?

Google Trends reported that hojicha searches reached an all-time high in 2026 and that “hojicha vs matcha” entered breakout growth. The expansion of Japanese-style café drinks appears to be moving interest beyond matcha toward less familiar roasted flavors.

Hojicha also works hot, iced, with milk, in ice cream, and in baking, allowing it to function as both a tea and a flavor in much the same way matcha expanded beyond the tea bowl.

The practical rule: choose matcha for vivid green color and grassy intensity from powdered tea; choose hojicha for a roasted, lower-astringency profile that works especially well with milk and very hot brewing water.

As a practical reference, adjust only one variable afterward: tea amount, water amount, temperature, or whisking intensity. Changing everything at once makes it difficult to know what produced a smoother flavor, stronger cup, or better texture.

faq.question: What is hojicha?
faq.answer: It is Japanese green tea that receives an additional roasting step, transforming its color and aroma.

faq.question: What does hojicha taste like?
faq.answer: It commonly has toasted grain, nut, caramel, woody, or lightly smoky notes with less bitterness and astringency.

faq.question: Is hojicha the same as matcha?
faq.answer: No. Matcha is a specific finely ground tea consumed as a suspension; hojicha is roasted tea traditionally brewed from leaves or stems.
